Pairs trading starts from a simple idea: two assets that move together over the long run generate a mean-reverting spread, tradable whenever it drifts from equilibrium. The problem is that markets don\'t hold that equilibrium steady: volatility clustering, correlations that collapse under stress, sudden regime shifts. Classical OLS-based techniques assume constant parameters over time, an assumption that doesn\'t survive contact with real data for long.

In my thesis I built an alternative framework that replaces static estimation with a dynamic one: a Kalman Filter updates the hedge ratio observation by observation, a GARCH model captures the spread\'s conditional variance, and a Hidden Markov Model detects latent market regimes to suspend trading when cointegration breaks down. The three components feed into a single adaptive z-score that drives entries and exits.

The framework was tested out-of-sample both in the bivariate case (classic pairs trading) and in its high-dimensional extension to multi-asset baskets. The bivariate case holds up across two independent experiments, including a dedicated test on the 2008-2009 crisis, with the regime gate visibly cutting drawdowns during stress periods. The multivariate extension doesn\'t generalize: the curse of dimensionality hits the Johansen cointegration test once the number of parameters grows faster than the available sample size, and no basket survives out-of-sample screening with thresholds inherited from the bivariate case.

The result isn\'t a clean win across the board, but it\'s the honest one: where the dynamic framework works, it protects capital better than static benchmarks; where it doesn\'t, the data says so plainly, and the reason lines up with what the theory predicted.
